items.title: US lawmakers criticize Nvidia decision to reinstate Huang as CEO
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's (NVDA.O) decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to the company's advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton, a Republican, on Monday called on Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, a bill that seeks to address legally exported advanced chips later being diverted to China, where their sales are restricted.

The bill would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users.

For Nvidia, the measure could create new compliance costs and reporting obligations.

Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is set to chair the Banking Committee starting in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "reckless," adding Nvidia's board still owes Congress answers about the company's compliance with US export controls. The Banking Committee is responsible for approving legislation on export controls.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," Warren said.

Huang will testify on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee in a public hearing, the panel's Republican Chair Tim Scott said Monday, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Huang's personal spokesperson declined to comment on the planned appearance.

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement on Monday that the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "doesn't excuse" him from testifying before Congress.

Ricketts is pushing for Congress to pass the Match Act, a bill that would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. It would not directly restrict Nvidia's chip sales.

Companies based in allied countries that make semiconductor-manufacturing tools would be affected, such as the Netherlands' ASML (ASML.AS) and Tokyo Electron (8035.T) in Japan.

Supporters argue that under the legislation, China would have greater difficulty developing its own advanced AI chips that would compete with Nvidia in the long term.

The top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, Representative Jim Himes, said Huang is still expected to appear for a closed-door interview on December 1 with three House panels.

Hakeem Jeffries, the incoming speaker of the US House of Representatives, said on Monday that Congress should include "ironclad" legislation to prevent AI technology from reaching China in the annual defense bill. That bill is a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of the legislation already includes several measures to crack down on China's access to advanced AI chips.

Nvidia did not immediately comment on the criticism from Congress.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said the reinstatement showed it was critical to pass legislation to toughen restrictions on US chip exports to China.

President Donald Trump on CNBC said he had pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang and that he did not think the board would have done so without his action.

Republican Senator John Curtis, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he wanted answers about why the board opted to reappoint Huang as CEO.

"Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him," he said. "I'd like to know what changed."

items.title: What to know about US Army plans to blow up a stockpile of lead azide in Iowa
items.content_html:
November 23 - The US Army plans to destroy 68 barrels, or nearly 10,000 pounds (4,536 kg), of a deteriorating lead compound used in explosives by detonating them at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

Nearby residents have protested and environmental groups filed a lawsuit, concerned about the likelihood that blowing up the lead azide will release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site.

Here is what you need to know:

WHAT IS LEAD AZIDE?

Lead azide is an explosive chemical used to detonate military munitions.

WHY IS THE ARMY PLANNING TO DETONATE IT?

The US Environmental Protection Agency said recrystallization in long-term storage made the chemical dangerously unstable, posing the risk of an uncontrolled explosion and making moving the material risky. In a court filing late on Saturday, the government said a controlled detonation was necessary "to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion."

The EPA on Saturday said there was an immediate risk that the lead azide would explode because temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 degrees Celsius) in Iowa this week.

WHEN COULD IT HAPPEN?

The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army's environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued. The Army said in a post on X on Sunday that the explosion would nonetheless take place on Wednesday, "to allow for optimal weather conditions." But in a Truth Social post on Monday President Donald Trump said he ordered the military to pause until it gets a ruling from the 8th Circuit allowing the detonation to go forward, making the timing uncertain.

The detonation was previously scheduled for November 20 and then postponed until Monday after public outcry.

WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, said immediate risks from inhalation should be mitigated if people are able to shelter or get away from the dust plume as it passes over them. Longer-term risks come from the settling of lead dust on homes, farms and in the environment, where it will not break down further.

Lead can cause wide-ranging health problems in humans and animals, O'Shaughnessy said. Children in particular are at risk because lead can inhibit the development of the brain and its cognitive abilities, he said.

The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has recommended that residents in affected areas keep windows and doors closed for 24–48 hours after the detonation and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air, clean surfaces in potentially affected areas after the detonation and consult healthcare providers about blood testing for lead.

WHO WILL BE AFFECTED?

The impact of the blast will depend largely on the weather forecast and the direction of the wind. O'Shaughnessy said a Wednesday detonation would likely create a plume of lead dust that would travel 40 to 50 miles (64 to 80 km) southwest of the military installation.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors to avoid direct lead exposure for livestock, while acknowledging that in some places, this would not be feasible.

IS THIS UNUSUAL?

The EPA says that explosive hazardous waste is "often treated by open burning and open detonation," but that disposing of such waste in enclosed environments is a preferred alternative that is becoming increasingly available.

Reporting by Renee Hickman; Editing by Donna Bryson and Bill Berkrot

items.title: Measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania rise to nine
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Pennsylvania Department of Health on Monday reported another death linked to this year's measles outbreak, taking the total number of fatalities associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine, from eight last week.

The latest death involved an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central Pennsylvania who tested positive for measles, the department said.

Pennsylvania has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far this year, including 330 hospitalizations, according to the health department.

The nine deaths reported this year involved residents of Centre, Clinton, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin and Montour counties. Lancaster County accounted for three deaths, while Jefferson County reported two.

Virginia on Friday reported its first measles-associated death of 2026, involving a child, while Wisconsin has reported two deaths. New York state has recorded one child death linked to the disease.

Based on publicly reported state figures, at least 13 measles-associated deaths have been recorded in the US this year.

However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, without specifying the states where the fatalities were recorded.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

The US Department of Health and Human Services said it was "saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania," adding that CDC has provided the state nearly $4 million in one-time emergency funding for response efforts in 2027.

Last week, the US lost its hard-fought measles elimination status after 26 years.

Nationwide, 5,838 confirmed measles cases were reported this year, as of November 19, according to CDC data.

"Most of the outbreaks of measles this year have been centered in counties where a lot of Amish and conservative Mennonites live," Kathryn Jacobsen, an epidemiologist at the University of Richmond, said, adding that large gatherings of unvaccinated people can allow the virus to spread rapidly.

Although the epidemic was currently centered in conservative, rural religious communities, she said this did not mean other groups were not at risk.

Reporting by Siddhi Mahatole and Kunal Das in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara, Shilpi Majumdar and Shinjini Ganguli

items.title: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk's SpaceX over Grok AI's creation of child sexual abuse images
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - Virginia and Oregon sued Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp (SPCX.O) on Monday, alleging the company profited from a feature in its AI model Grok that produces child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual sexual images from photographs while failing to put safeguards in place to stop it.

Several state attorneys general had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon were the first states to sue.

The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok's safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its "spicy mode." That mode allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.

Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.

In a statement posted on X on Monday that didn't directly address the lawsuits, the platform's safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate this type of imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it.

"The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards," the company posted.

GROK SAFEGUARDS UNDER SCRUTINY

Virginia's lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted on X millions of sexualized images, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

Investigators from the attorney general's office in Virginia found that Grok's image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.

Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images' creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.

States across the US have filed a growing number of lawsuits against social media and AI companies over harm they say the companies have caused to their residents.

In an interview with Reuters ahead of Monday's filings, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said state attorneys general are acting as a regulatory force in the tech industry, including on artificial intelligence, which has faced relatively little federal regulation so far.

"In the absence of federal action, AGs have stepped into the breach," Jones said.

LAWSUITS STACK UP OVER GROK

SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

In the UK, lawmaker Jess Asato is suing SpaceX after Grok users generated sexualized images of her. The company has denied the claims, arguing that obviously fictitious, AI-generated content cannot breach someone's right to privacy.

In mid-January, xAI said it restricted image editing in Grok and blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing "where it's illegal." SpaceX acquired xAI in February and rebranded its AI division from xAI to SpaceX Super Intelligence in October.

Reuters found in February that, even after new curbs, Grok continued to generate sexualized images of people even when users explicitly warned that the subjects did not consent. The company did not address detailed questions from Reuters about Grok's generation of sexualized material.

SpaceX is suing at least two people in the US alleging they misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

Reporting by Diana Novak Jones; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Will Dunham, Diane Craft and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: US agency to vote to ease ownership limits on local TV, radio stations
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Federal Communications Commission plans to vote next month to ease ownership limits on local radio and TV stations as it vows to level the playing field for broadcasters with large tech companies.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said the commission will vote on December 17 whether to lift the limits on the number of stations local broadcasters can own in the markets they operate in, replacing the limits with individual case-by-case reviews.

items.title: US Democrats require 2028 candidates to reject dark money to make debate stage
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US Democratic presidential hopefuls will be required to denounce election spending by secret donors to qualify for debates during the primary season, the party announced on Monday, as it braces for a potentially huge field of contenders.

The Democratic National Committee, which oversees the party's presidential primary process, is planning 12 debates that will help choose its 2028 White House standard-bearer.

So many contenders are expected to enter that the party has built provisions in for some debates to be held over two nights, with a maximum of 20 candidates in total taking part.

After their rout of Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats now face a potentially bruising presidential nominating battle, with no clear frontrunner yet.

At a gathering in Denver shortly after the elections, tensions between centrist Democrats and a restive progressive wing surfaced, underscoring long-standing ideological and generational divides as the party seeks a 2028 White House nominee.

To qualify for the Democratic presidential debates, candidates must sign a pledge denouncing "dark money" — political spending to influence elections by groups that do not disclose their donors.

The new requirement is part of a DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.

The DNC said it plans to hold five presidential primary debates in 2027 and seven in 2028.

The first two are scheduled for June and July 2027, while the final debate is expected to take place in March 2028, though the party said the schedule could be adjusted if needed. The locations of the early debates will be announced in January, the DNC said.

To demonstrate that they have voter support, candidates will also have to meet polling and grassroots fundraising requirements to qualify for the debates.

Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Paul Simao
